items.instruction: In this demonstration session, the adviser will build a fictional payment-reminder prompt live, thinking aloud at each step. You will see a weak version, an improved version, a version made worse by one specific change, and a peer example showing a different fictional case. All business, customer, invoice and amount details used in this session are entirely fictional and are used only as teaching illustrations. This session is a teaching demonstration, not an unannotated practice stimulus; it includes the adviser's reasoning, comparisons and tone-change explanation as part of the teaching. A separate Trainer would need to author a distinct unannotated practice stimulus if one is needed; none is created here. Follow along using the four materials: the explanation of prompt structure (mat-explanation-prompt-structure), the thinking-aloud transcript (mat-transcript-adviser-demo), the side-by-side weak/improved/worse comparison (mat-example-weak-improved-worse), and the peer failure illustration (mat-example-peer-failure).

materials.title: How a prompt is constructed: instruction, primary content and best practices
materials.content:
TEACHING EXPLANATION — PROMPT STRUCTURE

All business names, customer names, invoice details and amounts used in this explanation are entirely fictional and are used only as teaching illustrations.

──────────────────────────────────────
WHAT IS A PROMPT?
──────────────────────────────────────
When you use an AI writing tool, you communicate with it by typing a message called a prompt. The prompt is the text you send to the tool to tell it what you want. The quality and usefulness of what the tool produces depends significantly on how clearly and specifically that prompt is written.

This session focuses on two foundational building blocks that the source material (Prompt Engineering Fundamentals, wp3:32c2119d5504, excerpts 3 and 4) describes as the core of prompt construction:

1. INSTRUCTION — a direct statement telling the AI what action to perform.
2. PRIMARY CONTENT — the specific information the AI needs to act on.

The source also describes three further moves that build on these foundations:

3. EXAMPLE — one or more sample outputs supplied to show the AI the desired pattern. Supplying one example is called one-shot prompting; supplying more than one is few-shot prompting; supplying none is zero-shot prompting. (Source: excerpt 4 and excerpt 7.)
4. CUE — a leading word or phrase placed at the end of the prompt to nudge the AI toward a desired opening or format. (Source: excerpt 4.)
5. TEMPLATE — a reusable prompt structure containing placeholders that can be replaced with specific data for different uses. (Source: excerpts 4 and 6.)

The five-move label set (INSTRUCTION, PRIMARY CONTENT, EXAMPLE, CUE, TEMPLATE) is an operator adaptation of these source concepts for this workshop; it is not a verbatim source taxonomy or a validated instrument.

──────────────────────────────────────
BUILDING BLOCK 1: INSTRUCTION
──────────────────────────────────────
The source (excerpt 3) distinguishes a basic prompt — a minimal text input with no context — from an instruction prompt, which specifies a task in more detail. Compare:

Basic: "Write an email."
Instruction: "Write a polite but firm payment-reminder email."

The instruction version tells the AI what kind of email, what tone and what purpose. The source notes that adding context and instructions to a basic prompt improves the quality and relevance of the output, though the actual output will depend on the model, the system and the specific context — results vary and should be inspected.

──────────────────────────────────────
BUILDING BLOCK 2: PRIMARY CONTENT
──────────────────────────────────────
The source (excerpt 3) describes the primary content design pattern as dividing the prompt into two parts: an instruction (action) and relevant content (that influences action). Primary content is the specific information the AI should act on — the subject matter or data.

For a payment-reminder email, primary content might include:
- The fictional customer name
- The fictional invoice number and amount
- The fictional due date
- The requested action (e.g., arrange payment within five business days)

Without primary content, the AI has no specific data to work with and may produce a generic output that cannot be used without complete rewriting.

──────────────────────────────────────
BEST PRACTICES: BEING SPECIFIC AND CLEAR
──────────────────────────────────────
The source (excerpt 7) recommends: "Be specific and clear — Give more details about the desired context, outcome, length, format, style etc. This will improve both the quality and consistency of responses."

The source also recommends: "Be descriptive, use examples — Models may respond better to a 'show and tell' approach. Start with a zero-shot approach where you give it an instruction (but no examples) then try few-shot as a refinement, providing a few examples of the desired output."

Important caveat: the source (excerpt 6) notes that "models are stochastic by nature" and that prompt engineering is "a trial-and-error process." Adding details may improve output in many cases, but results depend on the model, the system context and the specific run. The same prompt may produce different outputs on different occasions. Inspect results rather than assuming a specific outcome.

──────────────────────────────────────
TONE GUIDANCE IN A PROMPT
──────────────────────────────────────
Including a tone instruction — such as "The tone should be calm and respectful" — is one way to give the AI guidance about the style of the output. Removing a tone instruction from a prompt removes that guidance. Whether and how the model responds to its absence depends on the model and context; the possible consequence is that the output may not reflect the desired tone, but no specific generated outcome can be guaranteed. This is illustrated in the worked examples in mat-example-weak-improved-worse.

──────────────────────────────────────
TEMPLATES AND REUSE
──────────────────────────────────────
The source (excerpt 6) describes templates as reusable prompt structures containing placeholders that can be replaced with data from various sources to generate a prompt dynamically. This allows creation of a library of reusable prompts. In this workshop, all placeholder data substituted into any template must be fictional.

──────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
──────────────────────────────────────
A well-constructed prompt typically includes at minimum:
- A clear INSTRUCTION stating what the AI should do
- Relevant PRIMARY CONTENT supplying the specific data it needs

Optionally it may include EXAMPLES (one-shot or few-shot), a CUE to guide the opening, and a TEMPLATE structure for reuse. All of these are illustrated in the transcript and examples that accompany this explanation. All details in those illustrations are fictional.

citations.supported_claim: The corpus defines prompt construction as instruction plus primary content (excerpts 3 and 4), describes examples/cues/templates and zero-shot/one-shot/few-shot distinctions (excerpts 4 and 7), covers reusable prompt libraries and domain-specific templates (excerpt 6), and recommends being specific and clear about context, outcome, length, format and style and notes model stochasticity and the trial-and-error nature of prompt engineering (excerpts 6 and 7).

materials.title: Thinking-aloud teaching transcript: adviser demonstration with fictional Stonebrook Tools case
materials.content:
TEACHING TRANSCRIPT — ADVISER DEMONSTRATION

This is a complete thinking-aloud teaching demonstration transcript. It is openly a teaching illustration and includes the adviser's reasoning, comparisons and tone-change explanation as part of the teaching. It is not an unannotated answer-free stimulus; a separate Trainer would need to author a distinct unannotated practice stimulus if one is needed. All business names, customer names, invoice details, amounts and dates in this transcript are entirely fictional and are used only as teaching illustrations.

Fictional business: Stonebrook Tools (fictional) — a small hand-tool wholesaler.
Fictional customer: Harbor Workshop (fictional).
Fictional invoice: DEMO-A-204 (fictional), amount EUR 86.40 (fictional), due date 9 May (fictional).
All details above are fictional. Any deadline mentioned is fictional prompt context, not a source mandate.

──────────────────────────────────────
LINE-NUMBERED TRANSCRIPT
──────────────────────────────────────

1.  Adviser: Right, let's build a prompt together from scratch. I'm going to think aloud at every step so you can see exactly why I'm making each choice. Everything I use today — the business name, the customer, the invoice — is entirely made up.

2.  Adviser: Here is my very first attempt at a prompt. I'm going to type exactly this:
    "Write an email about the invoice."
    That's it. Nothing else.

3.  Adviser: Now, what do you think the AI will do with that? There's no customer name, no invoice number, no amount, no date, no instruction about tone or length. The source material calls this a basic prompt — a minimal text input with no context. A basic prompt like this leaves almost everything for the model to decide.

4.  Adviser: So let me add the first building block: PRIMARY CONTENT. That means the specific information the AI needs to act on. I'm going to add the fictional customer name, the fictional invoice number, the fictional amount and the fictional due date. Watch the prompt grow:
    "Write a payment-reminder email to Harbor Workshop about invoice DEMO-A-204 for EUR 86.40, which was due on 9 May."

5.  Adviser: Already much more specific. The AI now knows who the email is going to, which invoice, how much and when it was due. But I still haven't told it what tone to use, or what I want the customer to do.

6.  Adviser: Now I'll add the INSTRUCTION layer — making it more specific about the task itself. Instead of just 'write an email', I'll say 'write a polite but firm payment-reminder email'. The source describes instruction prompts as specifying a task in more detail, providing better guidance to the AI.

7.  Adviser: I'll also add what action I want the customer to take — arrange payment within five business days — and I'll add a role context at the start, so the AI knows who it's supposed to be. Here is the improved prompt. I'm going to read it out in full:

    PROMPT TEXT
    You are a professional accounts assistant for Stonebrook Tools, a small hand-tool wholesaler. Write a payment-reminder email to Harbor Workshop about invoice DEMO-A-204 for EUR 86.40, which was due on 9 May. The tone should be friendly but firm. Ask the customer to arrange payment within five business days and include the invoice number and amount in the email body. Keep the tone calm and respectful.
    END PROMPT TEXT

8.  Adviser: Notice what I've added compared to the first attempt. I've given the AI a role — 'professional accounts assistant for Stonebrook Tools'. I've supplied all the primary content — customer name, invoice number, amount, due date. I've given a tone instruction — 'friendly but firm'. I've stated the requested action — 'arrange payment within five business days'. And I've ended with a tone-reinforcing sentence: 'Keep the tone calm and respectful.'

9.  Adviser: The source (excerpt 7) recommends being specific and clear — giving more details about the desired context, outcome, length, format and style. That's exactly what this improved prompt does compared to the first one.

10. Adviser: Now I want to show you what happens when we make one specific change that makes the prompt worse. I'm going to take the improved prompt and remove only the final sentence — 'Keep the tone calm and respectful.' — and leave everything else exactly as it is. Here is the worse prompt:

    PROMPT TEXT
    You are a professional accounts assistant for Stonebrook Tools, a small hand-tool wholesaler. Write a payment-reminder email to Harbor Workshop about invoice DEMO-A-204 for EUR 86.40, which was due on 9 May. The tone should be friendly but firm. Ask the customer to arrange payment within five business days and include the invoice number and amount in the email body.
    END PROMPT TEXT

11. Adviser: The only difference between the improved prompt and the worse prompt is the removal of that one sentence: 'Keep the tone calm and respectful.' Every other word, the customer name, the invoice number, the amount, the five-business-day deadline — all of that is identical.

12. Adviser: What is the possible consequence of removing it? The prompt still contains 'friendly but firm', so there is some tone guidance remaining. But removing 'Keep the tone calm and respectful' removes an additional, reinforcing tone instruction. The source (excerpt 6) notes that models are stochastic — they don't always produce the same output — and the source (excerpt 7) notes that prompt engineering is a trial-and-error process. Without that final sentence, the model has less explicit tone guidance. The output may or may not reflect a calm and respectful tone; we cannot predict a specific result. The possible consequence is loss of that tone guidance, which may matter in a customer-facing message. This is a tone-only detrimental change — no other element has been removed.

13. Adviser: This is the key teaching point about the worse prompt: a single, targeted removal of one sentence changes what guidance the model receives. It doesn't break the prompt, but it does reduce the specificity of the tone instruction.

14. Adviser: Now let me talk briefly about examples, cues and templates, because these are the other moves you can use.

15. Adviser: An EXAMPLE means actually supplying a sample output inside the prompt to show the AI the style you want. If you supply one example, that's called one-shot prompting. If you supply more than one, that's few-shot prompting. If you supply no examples at all, that's zero-shot prompting. In the prompts I've built today, I haven't included any sample email — so these are zero-shot prompts. The source (excerpt 7) notes: 'Start with a zero-shot approach where you give it an instruction (but no examples) then try few-shot as a refinement.' Whether adding examples improves the output depends on the model and the task; results should be inspected.

16. Adviser: A CUE is a leading word or phrase placed at the end of the prompt to nudge the AI toward a desired opening. For example, I could end my prompt with 'Dear Harbor Workshop,' and the AI would continue from there. I haven't used a cue in today's demonstration prompts.

17. Adviser: A TEMPLATE is a reusable prompt structure with placeholders — slots you fill in each time for different customers. For example: 'Write a payment-reminder email to [CUSTOMER NAME] about invoice [INVOICE NUMBER] for [AMOUNT]. Payment is due within five business days.' The brackets are the placeholders. When you use a template in this workshop, always substitute fictional details for every placeholder. Do not insert real customer names, real invoice numbers or real payment links.

18. Adviser: The source (excerpt 6) describes how templates with placeholders can be replaced with data from various sources to generate a prompt dynamically, and how this allows creation of a library of reusable prompts. That is the practical value of a template for a small business: you build it once and reuse it with different fictional — or in real use, real — customer details each time.

19. Adviser: To summarise what we've covered: I started with a basic prompt with no context, added primary content to give the AI the specific data it needs, added a more specific instruction and role context, and added tone guidance. I then showed how removing one sentence — the final tone-reinforcing sentence — is the only change between the improved and worse versions. I also mentioned examples (zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot), cues and templates. In the next material you will see the side-by-side comparison of the weak, improved and worse prompts, and then the peer failure example.

citations.supported_claim: The corpus describes basic prompts as minimal text inputs without context (excerpt 3), instruction plus primary content as the core construction pattern (excerpts 3 and 4), examples/cues/templates and zero-shot/one-shot/few-shot distinctions (excerpts 4 and 7), reusable prompt libraries and placeholders (excerpt 6), model stochasticity and trial-and-error iteration (excerpt 6), and best practices including being specific and clear about context, outcome, length, format and style (excerpt 7).

materials.title: Side-by-side comparison: weak, improved and worse prompts (fictional Stonebrook Tools case)
materials.content:
TEACHING EXAMPLE — SIDE-BY-SIDE PROMPT COMPARISON

This is a teaching illustration authored for this session. All business names, customer names, invoice details, amounts and dates are entirely fictional. The three prompts below are Teacher illustrations, not replacements for any assessment stimuli. The 'Keep the tone calm and respectful' sentence in the improved prompt is a fictional prompt-construction illustration; any deadline mentioned is fictional prompt context, not a source mandate.

Fictional business: Stonebrook Tools (fictional) — a small hand-tool wholesaler.
Fictional customer: Harbor Workshop (fictional).
Fictional invoice: DEMO-A-204 (fictional), amount EUR 86.40 (fictional), due date 9 May (fictional).

──────────────────────────────────────
VERSION 1 — WEAK PROMPT
──────────────────────────────────────
PROMPT TEXT
Write an email about the invoice.
END PROMPT TEXT

What is missing:
- No customer name (the AI does not know who to address)
- No invoice number, amount or due date (no primary content)
- No instruction about tone, action requested or role
- No guidance on length or format

This is what the source (excerpt 3) calls a basic prompt: a minimal text input with no context. Without primary content, the AI has no specific data to work with.

──────────────────────────────────────
VERSION 2 — IMPROVED PROMPT
──────────────────────────────────────
PROMPT TEXT
You are a professional accounts assistant for Stonebrook Tools, a small hand-tool wholesaler. Write a payment-reminder email to Harbor Workshop about invoice DEMO-A-204 for EUR 86.40, which was due on 9 May. The tone should be friendly but firm. Ask the customer to arrange payment within five business days and include the invoice number and amount in the email body. Keep the tone calm and respectful.
END PROMPT TEXT

What has been added compared to the weak prompt:
- Role context: 'You are a professional accounts assistant for Stonebrook Tools, a small hand-tool wholesaler.' This tells the AI who it is supposed to be.
- Specific instruction: 'Write a payment-reminder email' rather than just 'write an email'.
- Primary content: fictional customer name (Harbor Workshop), fictional invoice number (DEMO-A-204), fictional amount (EUR 86.40), fictional due date (9 May).
- Tone instruction: 'The tone should be friendly but firm.'
- Requested action: 'Ask the customer to arrange payment within five business days and include the invoice number and amount in the email body.'
- Tone-reinforcing closing sentence: 'Keep the tone calm and respectful.'

The source (excerpt 7) recommends being specific and clear — giving more details about the desired context, outcome, length, format and style. This improved prompt applies those principles. Note: the actual output will depend on the model, the system and the specific run; results vary and should be inspected.

──────────────────────────────────────
VERSION 3 — WORSE PROMPT
──────────────────────────────────────
PROMPT TEXT
You are a professional accounts assistant for Stonebrook Tools, a small hand-tool wholesaler. Write a payment-reminder email to Harbor Workshop about invoice DEMO-A-204 for EUR 86.40, which was due on 9 May. The tone should be friendly but firm. Ask the customer to arrange payment within five business days and include the invoice number and amount in the email body.
END PROMPT TEXT

The single change from the improved prompt:
The worse prompt is identical to the improved prompt except that the final sentence — 'Keep the tone calm and respectful.' — has been removed. Every other element — the role context, the customer name, the invoice number, the amount, the due date, the tone instruction 'friendly but firm', the five-business-day payment deadline, the instruction to include the invoice number and amount — is unchanged.

This is a tone-only detrimental change. No other element has been altered.

Possible consequence of the removal:
Removing 'Keep the tone calm and respectful.' removes a reinforcing tone instruction from the end of the prompt. The source (excerpt 6) notes that models are stochastic by nature, and the source (excerpt 7) notes that prompt engineering is a trial-and-error process. Without that final sentence, the model has less explicit tone guidance. The output may or may not reflect a calm and respectful tone; no specific generated outcome can be predicted or guaranteed. The possible consequence is loss of that tone guidance, which may matter for a customer-facing message.

──────────────────────────────────────
SIDE-BY-SIDE SUMMARY TABLE
──────────────────────────────────────
Element                          | Weak | Improved | Worse
Role context                     |  No  |   Yes    |  Yes
Specific instruction              |  No  |   Yes    |  Yes
Primary content (customer/inv.)  |  No  |   Yes    |  Yes
Tone instruction (friendly/firm) |  No  |   Yes    |  Yes
Requested action (5 bus. days)   |  No  |   Yes    |  Yes
Closing tone sentence             |  No  |   Yes    |  No  ← only difference between improved and worse

The closing tone sentence 'Keep the tone calm and respectful.' is the one and only difference between the improved and worse prompts.

citations.supported_claim: The corpus describes basic prompts as minimal text inputs without context (excerpt 3), notes model stochasticity and the trial-and-error nature of prompt engineering (excerpt 6), and recommends being specific and clear about context, outcome, length, format and style (excerpt 7), supporting a side-by-side comparison showing what is added in an improved prompt and what is lost when one element is removed.

materials.title: Peer failure illustration: fictional Cobalt Print Studio case (teaching illustration)
materials.content:
TEACHING EXAMPLE — PEER FAILURE ILLUSTRATION

This material presents a fictional peer example for teaching purposes. The email below is an authored illustration — it is not observed provider output, actual business experience or a real model response. It is labelled as an authored illustration throughout. All business names, customer names, invoice details and amounts are entirely fictional.

Fictional business: Cobalt Print Studio (fictional) — a small print and design studio.
Fictional customer: Elm Conference Services (fictional).
Fictional invoice: DEMO-P-317 (fictional), amount EUR 52.80 (fictional).
All details above are fictional.

──────────────────────────────────────
THE PEER'S FICTIONAL PROMPT
──────────────────────────────────────
The fictional peer used the following prompt:

"Chase up the client about money owed."

──────────────────────────────────────
WHAT THE PEER OBSERVED
──────────────────────────────────────
The fictional peer reported that the output she received was a very short, generic message. It did not include the customer's name, the invoice number, the amount owed or any payment deadline. She felt the message could not be sent to any customer without being completely rewritten.

──────────────────────────────────────
AUTHORED ILLUSTRATIVE EMAIL
──────────────────────────────────────
The following is a complete fictional email authored as a teaching illustration to show what a vague, generic output might look like in this situation. It is not an observed or recorded model output. It is labelled as an authored illustration.

ILLUSTRATIVE EMAIL
Subject: Payment Reminder

Dear Client,

I hope this message finds you well. I am writing to follow up regarding an outstanding payment that we have not yet received.

Could you please arrange for this to be settled at your earliest convenience? If you have any questions, do not hesitate to get in touch.

Kind regards,
Accounts Team
END ILLUSTRATIVE EMAIL

──────────────────────────────────────
TEACHING DIAGNOSIS
──────────────────────────────────────
This diagnosis is tied to the actual text of the peer's prompt and the illustrative email above.

The peer's prompt — "Chase up the client about money owed." — contains only a vague instruction and no primary content. Specifically:

1. No customer name: The prompt does not name the customer. The illustrative email therefore addresses the recipient only as 'Dear Client', which is not usable for a real business message to Elm Conference Services.

2. No invoice reference: The prompt contains no invoice number. The illustrative email contains no reference to invoice DEMO-P-317 or any invoice number, so the customer cannot identify which payment is being requested.

3. No amount: The prompt contains no amount. The illustrative email contains no figure, so the customer does not know how much is owed.

4. No deadline: The prompt contains no payment deadline. The illustrative email says only 'at your earliest convenience', which gives no specific timeframe.

5. Vague instruction: 'Chase up' and 'money owed' are informal and non-specific. The prompt does not specify the message type (payment-reminder email), the tone, or the action requested.

The source (excerpt 3) describes primary content as the specific information the AI needs to act on. The peer's prompt omits all primary content. The source (excerpt 7) recommends being specific and clear about context, outcome and style. The peer's prompt does neither.

Note: this illustrative email is an authored teaching illustration, not empirical evidence of a causal relationship between the prompt and a specific output. The source (excerpt 6) notes that models are stochastic. The illustration is used to make the teaching point visible, not to claim that this exact output would always result from this prompt. Different models, systems and runs may produce different outputs.

──────────────────────────────────────
KEY TEACHING POINT
──────────────────────────────────────
Compare the peer's prompt with the improved Stonebrook Tools prompt in mat-example-weak-improved-worse. The improved prompt names the customer, the invoice, the amount, the due date, the tone and the requested action. The peer's prompt names none of these. The difference in the specificity of the prompts is directly visible in the text of the two prompts. The possible consequence — a generic, unusable output — is illustrated by the authored email above, with the caveats about stochastic variation noted.

This peer example is a different fictional case from the assessment stimuli. It uses Cobalt Print Studio, Elm Conference Services and invoice DEMO-P-317. It does not reuse or solve any approved assessment prompt.

Corpus resources wp3:12ce471a0269 (grades 6–12 critical AI literacy) and wp3:4868ba8731b3 (AI in educational measurement) are not used as unit citations because they do not validate transfer to adult SME business learners and do not supply a SCN01 rubric or thresholds.
Notebook/API setup and illustrative lengths from corpus excerpts are not SCN01 requirements and are not imported into any material.

Source competency values are preserved without normalization: category DIGITAL, heRelevance HIGH, smeRelevance HIGH, vetRelevance HIGH are flagged as ENUM_VALUE mismatches; ksa SKILL and proficiency FOUNDATION are flagged as UNTYPED_VOCABULARY_VALUE mismatches. These are not repaired.
The GENERATED_CONTRACT missing-resources cardinality finding on LearningTarget_0 (Pointer1792169221668_USER_96) is left unrepaired.

The five-move taxonomy (INSTRUCTION, PRIMARY CONTENT, EXAMPLE, CUE, TEMPLATE) is an operator adaptation of source concepts for this workshop; it is not a verbatim source taxonomy or a validated instrument.

The improved demonstration prompt ends with the exact standalone sentence 'Keep the tone calm and respectful.' as required; the worse prompt is identical except that sentence is removed. This is a tone-only detrimental change. Any deadline in the fictional prompts is fictional prompt context, not a source mandate.

The illustrative email in mat-example-peer-failure is an authored teaching illustration, not observed provider output or empirical evidence of a causal relationship between a prompt and a specific output. Model stochasticity means different outputs are possible.
